passage:
Dear Lavanya,
It's been three weeks since you last replied. Before that, we talked every single night about everything: exams, your cat, my terrible drawing.
I've gone over every message I sent. Was it the joke about your brother? The day I didn't come to your recital? I've written and deleted about twenty messages. I felt stupid and sad, and honestly a bit scared that I'd done something awful without knowing.
So this is the only one I'm sending. If I hurt you, I'm sorry and I'd like to know. If you just need space, or if you've moved on, that's okay too. You don't owe me an explanation.
I'll still say hi in the corridor. I won't keep chasing you. I hope you're alright.
Joseph

qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.a: Joseph has felt confused, sad and a bit scared, replaying every message and wondering what went wrong.

You asked what happened with Kashish? Okay. I'm Charu, and I'll tell you how it went.
Kashish and I had been close since Class 7. Then in August she just stopped replying. No fight, nothing. Blue ticks, no answer.
I went crazy replaying stuff. Did I talk too much about my own problems? Was it the thing I said about her cousin? I'd lie awake scrolling our old chats, looking for the moment it went wrong. I almost sent message number forty.
My Didi stopped me. She said, "Write to her once, honestly. After that, let it be."
So I wrote: "Hey, I miss talking to you. If I did something, I'd like to know. If not, I'm here whenever." And that was it.
She never answered. It still stings sometimes. But I stopped blaming myself for every word. Some people drift, and you don't always get told why.

qa.a: In August.

qa.a: Charu felt confused and anxious, lying awake searching for what went wrong and blaming every word.

At the coaching hostel in Kota, everyone knew Rajni and Wasim talked every night on the common room phone and messaged all day. Then, one Monday, nothing. He stopped replying. He looked away in the corridor.
By Thursday Rajni felt like she'd been erased. She checked her phone every minute. At night she whispered to her roommate Sunita, "Maybe I'll make a new account. Just to see if he's online."
"No," Sunita said. "That will only hurt you more."
"Then what did I do wrong?"
"Maybe nothing. Some people vanish because they can't handle saying things. That's about him, not you."
Rajni cried into her pillow. Sunita didn't leave. The next evening, two other girls from their floor came to Rajni's room with chai and cards. They played until lights-out. Rajni still checked her phone once or twice. But the new account never got made.

Class teacher's note, Class 10A, Tuesday
Pallavi came to me upset during break. Her close friend Mohit had stopped replying to her messages and was avoiding her in class for two weeks. She asked if she had done something wrong.
I spoke to Mohit after school. He looked uncomfortable and said, "I just need some space. I didn't know how to say it without making her cry."
I asked him what silence feels like from the other side. He thought for a while and said, "Probably worse."
Together we talked about what a short, honest message could say. He wrote in his notebook: "Hey Pallavi, I'm sorry I went quiet. I've needed some space lately. It's not something you did. I'm still glad we're friends." He sent it before leaving.
Pallavi came to me the next morning. She was sad but calmer. "At least I know," she said. I'll check in with both of them next week.

qa.a: For two weeks.

Rukmini had dropped Harish without a word. Two years of sitting together in the school bus in Pune, and now she sat with the new girls from the dance club and looked straight past him.
Harish was furious. On the walk home he rehearsed replies in his head. Don't worry, I didn't even notice you were gone. Enjoy your new fake friends. Each one felt sharper than the last. He typed one out, thumb over the send button.
Then his little sister needed help with her maths homework, and by the time he got back to his phone, an hour had passed. The fury had cooled a little. The message looked childish.
He deleted it. He thought about whether the friendship mattered enough for one more try. It did.
He wrote: "Hey, I've missed sitting with you. If something changed, I'd rather hear it from you." He sent it, then put the phone face down and went to play football.

qa.a: In the school bus in Pune.

qa.q: How did Harish feel on the walk home?

I don't even know how to write this. This afternoon, someone screenshotted what I wrote in the class group about the science project, and cropped it so it looked like I was insulting Meghna. Then it was everywhere. Thirty-two messages in an hour. People I've never spoken to calling me fake. Someone made a sticker of my face.

Then I told Mummy and Chetan bhaiya at dinner. Mummy read it all, hugged me, and said, "Indu, this is not your fault." She emailed my class teacher tonight, and we're meeting the teacher at eight tomorrow.
I still feel exposed. But I'm not alone in it.

We didn't have phones, but we had a notebook that went round the back benches. One day someone drew a cartoon of Sebastian, the new boy, with huge ears and a joke about his old shirts. Tuan had set up the robotics club chat for their Melbourne school at the start of the year, which made him admin. He hadn't expected to like it so much. He could pin messages, mute people, remove them with one tap.
On Thursday, Rafael, the loudest boy in the club, messaged him privately: "Kick Oliver. His code crashed our robot at the demo. Everyone's annoyed."
Tuan looked at the member list. Oliver was quiet, new, and the only Year 8. Removing him would make Rafael happy. It would also humiliate Oliver in front of everyone.
Tuan felt the pull of it: the power to decide, the approval of the loud ones.
He wrote back: "Not removing anyone for a bug. That's what debugging is for." Then, in the main chat: "Team session on Friday to fix the code together. Oliver, want to walk us through it?"
Rafael sent an eye-roll. Oliver sent: "Yes!"

qa.q: Why did Rafael want Oliver removed?
qa.a: Oliver's code crashed their robot at the demo.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when Rafael asked him to kick Oliver?
qa.a: He felt the pull of power and the wish for the loud boys' approval, while also sensing it would humiliate Oliver.

qa.q: Which choice did Tuan make as admin, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He refused to remove Oliver for a bug and invited him to lead a fixing session, using his power fairly instead of to humiliate.

qa.q: How might Rafael see Tuan's decision?
qa.a: Rafael seems annoyed, sending an eye-roll, because he wanted Oliver gone and didn't get his way.

grounding: A teen group admin enjoys the power to remove people but uses it fairly instead of excluding someone to please the loud ones.
